recent_posts.title: 0$ Marketing, Steam Demos & Custom Game Engine
recent_posts.summary: An indie game developer discusses building Gnomes, a tower defense roguelike, in 10 months using a custom Rust engine. The conversation covers technical decisions like choosing custom engines over established frameworks, the importance of gameplay-first design, and practical marketing strategies including treating demos as launches, leveraging Reddit for zero-budget promotion, and targeting Steam's new and trending algorithm. Key insights include balancing economy-driven gameplay, the trade-offs between solo and team development, and why limiting scope while deepening core mechanics leads to more marketable games.

recent_posts.title: Industry Veteran About Coding for Games
recent_posts.summary: Rick Pelosu, co-founder of Epic Tellers with 20+ years in AAA game development, shares insights on coding philosophy for games. He emphasizes simplicity over complexity, advocates against over-architecting systems upfront, and values practical solutions that solve immediate problems. Key themes include the importance of readable code, managing team dynamics in large studios, the role of luck in success, and why experience doesn't always transfer between projects. He discusses working with Godot on a 30+ person remote team and explains how game development differs significantly from studio to studio, with no universal formula for success.

recent_posts.title: Why game development formulas become fuzzier with experience
recent_posts.summary: Game developers discuss how their understanding of what makes successful games becomes less formulaic with experience. They explore the balance between appeal and retention, the importance of scope management, and how creativity works as a remixing process rather than pure creation. The conversation covers practical advice like starting with small projects, building intuition through consuming diverse media, and making strategic execution decisions. Using the development of 'Slots and Daggers' as a case study, they demonstrate how combining proven mechanics (slot machines + roguelike deck builders) with efficient art direction can create compelling games quickly.

recent_posts.title: Building nonviolent open world games with detailed environments and quest design
recent_posts.summary: Interview with Danny Weinbaum from Eastshade Studios about creating nonviolent narrative adventure games. Covers the 5-year development of Eastshade (grossing ~$4M), environment art techniques using trim sheets and GPU instancing, quest design philosophy emphasizing multi-stage complexity, performance optimization strategies for open-world games, and the business side of indie development including voice acting costs and launch preparation.

recent_posts.title: Grinding Steam Review Guesser On Hard Mode
recent_posts.summary: A game developer shares their experience playing a custom-built Steam review guessing game on hard mode, where players predict review counts based on store page information. The creator released the tool as open source on GitHub, inviting others to modify and use it. The video demonstrates gameplay while analyzing factors that influence game success, including polish level, content depth, pricing, release timing, and genre popularity. Through trial and error, patterns emerge about what drives review counts on Steam.

recent_posts.title: Solo dev built viral Steam hit in 4 months working 3 hours daily
recent_posts.summary: Solo developer Zoro Arts shares how he built Pedal Pedal Pedal, a viral co-op game that sold 120,000+ units, in just 4 months while studying at university. Working only 3 hours daily, he created a demo in 2 weeks that gained massive social media traction. The conversation covers his journey from his first commercial game Maky's Adventure, learning Unity networking with Photon, dealing with feature creep, working with publisher Assemble Entertainment, and his philosophy of making fun games quickly rather than spending years on single projects. He emphasizes gameplay over graphics, rapid prototyping, and using social media feedback to validate ideas early.

recent_posts.title: How an indie studio grew through three games and eight years of lessons
recent_posts.summary: Steven Huang, founder of ISTO Inc., shares his indie game studio's 8-year journey from commercial failure to gradual success. Starting with a 3-year mobile puzzle game that earned $30k, the team learned critical lessons about genre selection, market validation, and scope management. Their second game, Atrio (an automation-survival hybrid), took 5 years but suffered from mixing genres and abstract hooks, though it achieved sustainability. The breakthrough came with their third game, Get to Work, built in just one year using reusable code systems and strategic streamer partnerships. Key insights include: validate ideas early with players, choose proven genres over innovation when starting out, build reusable systems across projects, and leverage YouTube/streaming for marketing momentum.

recent_posts.title: Making a Cozy Game Hit in 5 Months
How a four person team built Dorfromantik from prototype to indie hit
recent_posts.summary: Toukana Interactive's founders discuss their journey from game school students to successful indie developers. They share how Dorfromantik went from a game jam prototype to a hit that sold thousands of copies in hours, eventually spawning an award-winning board game. The team explains their cautious approach to prototyping, performance optimization challenges (especially GPU instancing and Switch porting), and their philosophy of staying small while maintaining team culture. They detail their collaboration with Kurzgesagt on their second game Starbirds, revealing lessons about scope management and the importance of well-defined core mechanics.
